case_name: CASE OF KHADIJA ISMAYILOVA v. AZERBAIJAN (No. 4)

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant’s criminal conviction, imprisonment, and subsequent probationary restrictions (see paragraphs 11, 16, 19) directly stemmed from her journalistic activities, including her role at Azadliq Radio and her investigative work. Such measures constitute a clear interference with her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention, as criminal sanctions for journalistic conduct have been recognized as interferences in the Court’s jurisprudence (see no. 65286/13).
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference was grounded in domestic law, specifically Articles 192 and 213 of the Criminal Code, as well as the Law on Media (see paragraphs 10, 21-24, 29). The applicant’s conviction was imposed by the domestic courts applying these statutory provisions (see paragraphs 11, 14-16), and the legal framework itself was accessible and foreseeable, satisfying the requirement of lawfulness under Article 10(2).
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The stated purpose of the interference was the prevention of crime, particularly illegal entrepreneurship and tax evasion (see paragraphs 10, 21-23). The prevention of crime is explicitly listed as a legitimate aim under Article 10(2) of the Convention, and the domestic authorities relied on this justification (see no. 43579/98).
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference fails the necessity test. Firstly, there was no pressing social need for criminal prosecution, as the charges were based on technical violations (e.g., accreditation and tax classification) rather than concrete harm (see paragraphs 10, 12-13). Secondly, the authorities did not pursue the least restrictive means; administrative or civil remedies would have sufficed for any genuine regulatory concerns. Thirdly, the domestic courts provided insufficient reasoning, failing to address the applicant’s arguments that the charges lacked a valid legal basis for her journalistic activities (see paragraphs 13-16). The Court has held that criminal sanctions against journalists require compelling justification, particularly when their work involves public interest reporting (see no. 28396/95). Here, the measures were disproportionate and lacked convincing reasons, rendering them unnecessary in a democratic society.
